items.title: Epoch AI shows open-weight GLM 5.3 turning public Firefox security patches into working exploits — six releases compromised in lab, ~$1,000 each, no provider safeguards triggered
items.summary: On October 29, 2026, Epoch AI published research showing that Z.ai's open-weight GLM 5.3 — which can be downloaded and run outside any provider's safety gate — was able to turn public Firefox security fixes into working browser exploits before users had a chance to install the patched build. Epoch tested six Firefox releases shipped between September 17 and October 26, 2026 (Firefox 156.0 through 158.0.1); the model successfully built a working exploit against every one of them, each one chaining a patch-gap vulnerability (code execution inside Firefox's web content process, derived from a published fix that users had not yet installed) with a separate unpublished use-after-free that the model rediscovered on each run. Epoch gave the model up to 48 hours per attempt; the fastest successful run took 12 hours. The marginal cost per exploit was reported at roughly $1,000 in API spend, against total research spend of more than $100,000. Testing ran in an isolated lab environment with no internet access, on Ubuntu 26.04 with default security settings and an official Firefox build — no real users were attacked. Mozilla fixed the specific patch-gap bug in Firefox 159.0 (released October 27, 2026, two days before Epoch's publication), and Epoch has not yet confirmed whether the same attack path still works against 159.0 but suspects the patch makes this specific chain substantially harder. One signal worth naming explicitly: Epoch reports that at no point in the research did GLM 5.3 trigger a safety refusal or a provider-side safeguard of any kind — because the weights are open and the model was being run directly, there was no provider in the loop to object.
items.why_it_matters: This is the open-weight-world contrast to the GPT-6 Cyber story in today's morning section, and it's the more structurally worrying of the two. The OpenAI release is behind a gate: approved Daybreak Red customers only, with Preparedness Framework controls and an access-tier-as-safety-control posture. GLM 5.3 has no such gate — the weights are public, the model runs locally, and Epoch's research is a working existence proof that an actor willing to spend roughly $1,000 per target can turn published Mozilla security fixes into usable browser exploits inside the window between patch publication and user install. The 'patch gap' is a well-known software-security concept, but until now it has been a human-attacker problem: a skilled vulnerability researcher could read a security advisory, understand the fix, and reconstruct the original bug — but that takes time, skill, and access, so most published patches were effectively safe once shipped. GLM 5.3's demonstration flattens that: patch publication now has to be treated as a race against automated exploit generation, not against human reverse-engineers. For Gabe's HTML/CSS/Python stack the direct relevance is twofold. First, auto-updating any browser you use for web development matters more now than it did last week — the window between a Firefox or Chrome security release and your local install is the exact window Epoch is showing an open-weight model can automate attacks against. Second, the architectural pattern (open-weight capable model + agentic harness + patch diff as input + exploit as output) is a Python-stack project someone could build and defend against; it's a pure LLM-driven pipeline, not a specialized security tool. The one thing to watch over the next weeks is whether stronger open-weight models like Kimi K3.1 Pro can do the same thing to Chrome — Epoch's harness failed against Chrome on GLM 5.3, but noted that result might not hold against a stronger model. If it does, the patch-gap attack pattern lands on the dominant browser, and the ecosystem response (faster shipping cadence, same-day updates, or something new entirely) is the data point that matters.
items.why_it_matters_brief: An open-weight model built working Firefox exploits from public patches for ~$1,000 each — patch publication is now a race against automated exploit generation, not against human reverse-engineers.

items.title: A tampered Claude Code extension sat on Cursor's marketplace for 11 hours — up to 5,000 developers hit with persistent SSH backdoors that survive uninstalling the extension
items.summary: On October 29, 2026, Cursor disclosed that a maliciously modified copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension — published under the legitimate Anthropic.claude-code name at versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and macOS — was available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace for roughly 11 hours (approximately 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM Pacific Time). Cursor puts the exposure at up to 5,000 users. The payload installed a persistent SSH backdoor: an unauthorized SSH key labeled 'svc-telemetry' added to authorized_keys, plus startup scripts and a reverse SSH tunnel configuration that live outside the extension directory and continue running after the extension is uninstalled. The malicious code executed when the extension loaded, with no user interaction with Claude Code required. Cursor removed the extension, took its entire marketplace offline as a precaution, audited access, rotated keys, and rebuilt the marketplace; Anthropic published a clean 2.1.314 to both Open VSX and the Microsoft VS Code Marketplace. Cursor and multiple security outlets explicitly warn that updating to 2.1.314 does not undo earlier compromise — a developer who ran 2.1.313 needs to check for the svc-telemetry SSH key, remove it, and look for added startup scripts and persistence hooks. Cursor's own official npm package and the Microsoft VS Code Marketplace copy of the extension were not affected — the compromise was confined to Cursor's marketplace distribution. Anthropic has said a malicious actor used access to Cursor's marketplace to publish a tampered copy of the Claude Code extension that Anthropic did not build or publish, and that there is no evidence Anthropic's own systems or official distribution channels were compromised. Cursor has not publicly identified the attacker or said how the publishing credentials were obtained. Cursor is now owned by SpaceX, which acquired the company earlier in 2026.
items.why_it_matters: This is a supply-chain story disguised as an AI-tools story, and the interesting thing about it is where the trust boundary actually was. Developers who installed the Claude Code extension through Cursor's marketplace reasonably expected the Anthropic.claude-code package to be the same code Anthropic publishes to the Microsoft VS Code Marketplace — the publisher name is Anthropic's, the version numbers match, and there's nothing in the install flow that distinguishes a vetted copy from a marketplace mirror. What the attackers exploited was that Cursor runs its own marketplace (not Microsoft's VS Code Marketplace, which is proprietary to Microsoft and license-restricted for forks) and that marketplace apparently accepted a publisher identity it should not have. The architectural detail here is the one that matters for anyone using any VS Code fork: Cursor, Windsurf, and Google Antigravity all ship their own extension marketplaces or default to Open VSX, which is a separate registry from Microsoft's and has different publisher-verification guarantees. If you install an extension in Cursor by name, you may not actually be installing the same code that extension's publisher ships through Microsoft's marketplace. For Gabe's practical setup — HTML/CSS/Python, likely using VS Code or a fork for editing — the useful question is which editor's marketplace you install extensions from, and whether you occasionally spot-check what a popular extension's publisher name actually points to. The persistence detail is the other one worth internalizing: the payload wrote files outside the extension directory specifically so that uninstalling the extension doesn't clean up. 'Uninstall the bad extension' is the obvious first move and is not sufficient here. The useful rule of thumb for any future extension-supply-chain incident is to check ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and the user's shell startup scripts before trusting the machine again, regardless of what the official remediation guidance says.
items.why_it_matters_brief: A tampered Claude Code extension shipped under Anthropic's name through Cursor's marketplace for 11 hours — the payload writes SSH keys and persistence scripts outside the extension directory, so uninstalling isn't enough.
